paragraphs: Auction design seeks rules that encourage truthful bidding while maximizing the seller’s expected revenue. Designing these rules becomes difficult when several items are sold together. Earlier learning approaches described in the paper either assume a fixed collection of bidders and items or require symmetry, restricting the kinds of auctions they can represent.

CITransNet incorporates publicly available information about bidders and items into a transformer-based auction model. Its permutation equivariance means that reordering bids and their associated context produces a corresponding reordering of the output. This preserves consistency under changes in input order while still allowing asymmetric solutions informed by context. Order consistency and differentiated treatment can therefore coexist within the same architecture.

Experiments show that the model recovers known optimal mechanisms in single-item settings, beats strong baselines in multi-item settings, and generalizes to cases outside training. These findings support contextual auction learning as a way to expand the mechanisms a neural architecture can discover; they do not establish optimality for every multi-item auction.
icml-2022-a-context-integrated-transform.tldr: CITransNet uses bidder and item context to learn flexible auction mechanisms with strong experimental revenue-design results.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization often uses a stream of data to improve a model step by step. Here, that stream comes from a Markov chain, so successive observations can depend on one another. The chain’s mixing time describes how quickly it loses dependence on its starting state. Existing methods in this setting require that quantity, although it is usually unknown in applications.

The paper combines multi-level Monte Carlo gradient estimation with an adaptive learning method. Together, these components allow optimization without supplying the mixing time beforehand. For convex problems, the method attains the optimal asymptotic convergence rate. The result concerns long-run convergence behavior while removing a piece of information that earlier methods relied on.

The authors also extend the approach to finding stationary points in non-convex problems and to temporal difference learning, where they improve dependence on mixing time. Both extensions remain unaware of the mixing time itself. The central contribution is therefore adaptation to correlated data without requiring an advance estimate of how quickly that correlation dissipates.
icml-2022-adapting-to-mixing-time-in-sto.tldr: An adaptive optimization method handles Markovian data without knowing its mixing time and achieves optimal asymptotic convergence for convex problems.

paragraphs: Learning can improve combinatorial solvers, but obtaining training labels may itself require solving expensive problems. This paper investigates whether contrastive pre-training can reduce that burden for Boolean satisfiability. The underlying challenge is to learn useful representations from transformed versions of problem instances before relying heavily on labeled examples.

The authors focus on how those transformations are chosen. Common graph augmentations do not account for labels, whereas combinatorial problems often have known invariances: changes that preserve the answer. The study uses such invariances to construct label-preserving augmentations. This matters because treating two transformed instances as related is useful only when the transformation respects the information the eventual task needs.

The experiments find that preserving labels is critical to successful contrastive pre-training in this setting. The resulting representations reach test accuracy comparable to fully supervised learning while using only 1% of the labels. They also transfer better to larger problems from previously unseen domains. The findings identify augmentation design as a substantive part of learning combinatorial structure.
icml-2022-augment-with-care-contrastive-.tldr: Label-preserving augmentations make contrastive learning effective for satisfiability problems, achieving comparable supervised accuracy with only 1% of the labels.

paragraphs: Topic models uncover hidden semantic structure in collections of documents. Deep topic models can do this effectively, but they typically need many documents to learn useful patterns. This paper addresses the setting where a task provides only a small amount of text, making it difficult to learn its topics from scratch.

The framework combines two ideas. A generative model with two levels uses task information to guide how documents are modeled. A topic meta-learner learns shared topic embeddings that can be adapted into task-specific embeddings using only a few examples. The shared representations provide reusable topic knowledge, while adaptation allows the model to account for the particular task’s documents.

The authors implement this framework within a hierarchical embedded topic model. Across experiments, it outperforms several baseline models on few-shot topic discovery and few-shot document classification. These results support learning an adaptable foundation for topics when individual tasks have little data, with benefits for both uncovering themes and using text representations to classify documents.
icml-2022-bayesian-deep-embedding-topic-.tldr: A topic meta-learner adapts shared topic embeddings to small document collections, improving few-shot topic discovery and classification.

paragraphs: A mobile robot opening office doors must combine perception with physical action. Adding RGB and depth cameras supplies complementary information, but it also creates multiple ways for simulated sensor inputs to differ from real ones. The paper studies Bayesian imitation learning as a way to improve this transfer while making use of several sensors.

The method regularizes convolutional networks with a Variational Information Bottleneck. The authors find that this improves generalization to held-out domains and reduces the simulation-to-reality gap across sensor types. The learned embeddings also provide estimates of each sensor’s model uncertainty. These estimates help the policy combine RGB and depth information according to how uncertain each sensor is in the current situation.

In a real office environment, the method achieves 96% task success, with the abstract reporting a +16% improvement over its baseline. The contribution connects representation regularization with uncertainty-aware sensor fusion: the learned representation supports transfer, while its uncertainty information helps the robot use multiple inputs under changing conditions.
icml-2022-bayesian-imitation-learning-fo.tldr: Bayesian representation learning improves simulation-to-reality transfer and uncertainty-aware sensor fusion for a door-opening robot.

paragraphs: Standard episodic reinforcement learning follows one sequence of states and actions. Branching reinforcement learning instead allows several base actions at a state, each leading to successor states. An episode consequently forms a tree rather than a single path. This formulation is motivated by applications including hierarchical recommendation and online advertising.

A tree can grow exponentially with its depth, raising the question of whether learning must become correspondingly expensive. The paper develops Bellman equations and supporting value and variance identities for this branching structure. A key result bounds total variance by O(H²), where H is the episode depth, despite the potentially exponential number of nodes in a trajectory.

The authors propose BranchVI for regret minimization and BranchRFE for reward-free exploration. Both algorithms are computationally efficient, and their regret or sample-complexity guarantees are polynomial in all problem parameters. Nearly matching upper and lower bounds further characterize the difficulty of the model. These results show that exponentially large trajectories need not force exponentially large learning requirements in this formulation.
icml-2022-branching-reinforcement-learni.tldr: Branching reinforcement learning models tree-shaped episodes and admits efficient algorithms with polynomial learning guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to retain a useful small summary when some of its elements may later be deleted by an adversary. Usefulness is measured by a monotone submodular objective, which captures increasing value with diminishing returns. A matroid constraint specifies which selected subsets are feasible. The summary must still contain a high-value feasible selection after deletions.

The authors give constant-factor approximation algorithms for centralized and streaming settings. Their storage requirements depend on the matroid rank k and the deletion budget d. Both use summary size O(k + (d/ε²) log(k/ε)); the streaming algorithm also has this memory bound. This makes the retained information explicitly responsive to both selection capacity and the number of losses it must withstand.

The centralized approximation factor is 3.582 + O(ε), while the streaming factor is 5.582 + O(ε). These are bounded-quality guarantees rather than promises of exact optimization after deletion. Experiments on real-world datasets also demonstrate effectiveness, complementing the theoretical tradeoff between compact storage and resilience.
icml-2022-deletion-robust-submodular-max.tldr: Compact summaries preserve provably good submodular selections under adversarial deletions, in both centralized and streaming settings.

paragraphs: A discrete graphical model represents variables with discrete states and interactions between them. Maximum a posteriori inference seeks the most probable joint assignment. This paper develops low-rank semidefinite-programming bounds for that problem, covering models with arbitrary numbers of states and arbitrary pairwise interaction potentials. The focus is on computing bounds for a discrete optimization problem.

The method extends a Burer–Monteiro-style approach, using a low-rank representation in the bound computation. The authors examine two ways to handle constraints. One introduces penalties, while the other uses a dedicated block coordinate descent procedure. The latter avoids putting large penalty coefficients into the cost matrix, addressing a concrete issue with the penalty-based formulation.

The paper establishes that its algorithm is decreasing, meaning its objective progresses downward during optimization. This property does not by itself assert that the procedure finds a global optimum. Experiments favor block coordinate descent over both the penalized alternative and conventional linear bounds based on convergent message passing. The results support this approach as an effective way to compute graphical-model bounds.
icml-2022-efficient-low-rank-convex-boun.tldr: A low-rank semidefinite approach computes graphical-model inference bounds using block coordinate descent that avoids large constraint penalties.

paragraphs: An inductive bias favors certain kinds of solutions, such as sparse ones that depend on relatively few variables. When the true signal is sparse, a strong preference for sparsity may seem naturally beneficial. This paper shows why that intuition needs care when a model interpolates noisy data, fitting the training examples exactly.

The tension is that a stronger structural preference can align the fitted model with the true signal while also increasing the damage caused by fitting noise. For linear regression and classification with sparse ground truth, the authors analyze minimum ℓp-norm and maximum ℓp-margin interpolators. They prove fast polynomial rates close to 1/n for p greater than 1, compared with a logarithmic rate at p equal to 1.

The result challenges the idea that stronger alignment with the signal’s structure always improves generalization in noisy interpolation. It does not overturn that intuition for regularized models. Preliminary experiments suggest that the same tradeoff may help explain nonlinear interpolating models, but that extension is presented as exploratory evidence.
icml-2022-fast-rates-for-noisy-interpola.tldr: For noisy interpolation with sparse ground truth, stronger sparsity bias can amplify noise and produce much slower learning rates.

paragraphs: Quantization represents neural-network weights with fewer bits, reducing memory and computational demands. It also changes the distribution of weights relative to the original network, which can harm performance. This paper approaches that mismatch statistically, learning a low-bit representation that is guided by the task rather than relying on several manually chosen configurations.

The method learns a latent sub-distribution within the model and smoothly approximates it using a Gaussian mixture. Network weights are projected according to that approximation. As training updates the weights, the sub-distribution changes alongside them, with both driven by the task objective. The mapping used for quantization is therefore part of the learning process.

Experiments on image classification and object detection across multiple architectures support the method’s effectiveness, generalization, and transferability. The authors also develop a mobile-CPU deployment flow and report up to 7.46× inference acceleration on an octa-core ARM processor. That deployment result connects the learned low-bit representation to measured execution speed, with the reported maximum tied to the evaluated setting.
icml-2022-finding-the-task-optimal-low-b.tldr: Adaptive Gaussian-mixture quantization jointly learns low-bit weight mappings and network weights, with reported mobile-CPU speedups up to 7.46×.

paragraphs: Images and other measurements are commonly stored on discrete grids, even when the signal they describe is continuous. An implicit neural representation instead encodes a measurement as a neural function that maps spatial locations to values. This paper asks how to perform learning when those functions themselves become the data points, calling them functa.

Making that shift requires more than fitting a separate function to each observation. The framework addresses efficient conversion into functa, compact storage of the resulting representations, and learning downstream tasks from them. Its central idea is to organize the learning pipeline around functional representations of measurements rather than their original grid-based form.

The authors apply their recipe to images, three-dimensional shapes, neural radiance fields, and data on manifolds. They demonstrate useful properties in generative modeling, filling in missing data, synthesizing novel views, and classification. These demonstrations establish the breadth of the proposed representation strategy across several modalities and tasks, without claiming that function-based data universally outperforms every discrete representation.
icml-2022-from-data-to-functa-your-data-.tldr: The functa framework treats neural functions as data points and supports learning across images, shapes, radiance fields, and manifolds.

paragraphs: Larger language models have delivered strong results, but increasing the size of dense models also demands substantial computation. GLaM explores a different way to expand capacity: a sparsely activated mixture of experts. The architecture contains many parameters while activating only part of its expert capacity for computation, separating total model size from how much is used at once.

The paper develops a family of models built around this design. Its largest model contains 1.2 trillion parameters, approximately seven times GPT-3’s parameter count. In the reported comparison, it uses one-third of the energy required to train GPT-3 and half the inference floating-point operations. These figures describe different resource measures rather than a single interchangeable notion of cost.

Despite those reductions, the model achieves better overall few-shot performance across 29 natural-language-processing tasks. The finding supports sparse activation as a practical route to greater capacity with lower reported training energy and inference computation. Better overall performance describes the aggregate comparison; it does not assert improvement on every task.
icml-2022-glam-efficient-scaling-of-lang.tldr: GLaM scales language-model capacity through sparse experts, reporting better overall few-shot performance than GPT-3 with lower training energy and inference computation.

paragraphs: Self-attention connects information across a sequence, including positions far apart. This paper asks a more specific theoretical question: which functions and long-range dependencies does the architecture favor representing? That focus concerns inductive bias, the preferences built into a model that influence what it can learn efficiently from examples.

The main result applies to Transformer networks with bounded norms. Under that condition, a single attention head can represent a sparse function of the input sequence. Here, sparsity means that the function depends on a limited part of the sequence. The associated sample complexity grows only logarithmically with context length, so the bound increases slowly as the surrounding sequence becomes longer.

The authors describe this capability as creating sparse variables: attention can form representations of selected input dependencies. Synthetic experiments examine learning sparse Boolean functions and support the theoretical analysis. The contribution gives a precise account of one useful preference of self-attention, with the bounded-norm condition and sparse-function setting central to the stated result.
icml-2022-inductive-biases-and-variable-.tldr: Bounded-norm Transformers can represent sparse sequence functions with sample complexity growing only logarithmically with context length.

paragraphs: Many neural networks use a computational budget fixed by their architecture, even when some inputs require substantially more reasoning than others. This paper develops a framework in which solving a problem involves repeated refinement. The motivation is to make additional computation available for difficult algorithmic tasks instead of requiring every answer to emerge from the same fixed amount of processing.

A neural network learns an energy landscape over candidate outputs. Each reasoning step attempts to reduce energy, moving toward a low-energy solution. For harder problems with more complex landscapes, the framework allows a more complex optimization procedure and therefore a different computational budget. This is a mechanism for adjusting effort, rather than a guarantee that extra optimization always finds the correct answer.

Experiments illustrate improved accuracy and generalization on algorithmic reasoning tasks in graph and continuous domains. The authors also demonstrate recursive solutions to problems requiring nested reasoning. These findings support energy minimization as a way to organize iterative computation and reuse it within more complex reasoning procedures.
icml-2022-learning-iterative-reasoning-t.tldr: A learned energy landscape turns neural reasoning into iterative optimization, allowing computational effort to be adjusted for harder problems.

paragraphs: Searching for drug-like molecules that bind strongly to a target protein is expensive, especially when evaluating candidates requires costly physics-based calculations. LIMO accelerates this search by optimizing within a learned molecular representation. Its aim is to generate promising structures while making property-directed search faster.

The method uses a variational autoencoder’s latent space and two neural networks arranged in sequence for property prediction. This arrangement enables gradient-based reverse optimization: desired molecular properties guide changes in the latent representation. Experiments show competitive performance on benchmark tasks and stronger results than leading methods on the evaluated task of generating drug-like molecules with high predicted binding affinity.

Docking-based results reach nanomolar affinity against two protein targets. The authors further support these findings using molecular-dynamics calculations of absolute binding free energy. One generated compound has a predicted dissociation constant of 6 × 10⁻¹⁴ M against the human estrogen receptor. These are computational affinity findings, with the stronger calculation providing additional evidence for candidates produced by the faster search.
icml-2022-limo-latent-inceptionism-for-t.tldr: LIMO uses gradient-based optimization in a molecular latent space to accelerate generation of compounds with strong computationally predicted binding affinity.

paragraphs: Algorithmic recourse recommends actions someone can take to obtain a favorable decision from a classifier. A recommendation is less useful if small uncertainty in that person’s recorded features causes it to fail. This paper formalizes recourse that must withstand such uncertainty, treating robustness as part of the recommendation problem.

The authors show that methods offering minimally costly recourse fail to be robust. This reveals a tension between finding the cheapest change and finding one whose success survives small feature perturbations. They then develop methods for producing adversarially robust recourse for linear classifiers and for differentiable classifiers, addressing robustness directly rather than considering only action cost.

The paper also examines how the classifier itself can make reliable recourse easier to obtain. Regularizing it to behave locally like a linear model and to rely more heavily on actionable features facilitates the existence of robust recommendations. This finding connects decision-model design with recourse quality: robustness depends partly on how the classifier uses information, as well as on the recommendation procedure.
icml-2022-on-the-adversarial-robustness-.tldr: The paper develops recourse methods robust to feature uncertainty and shows how classifier design can help such recommendations exist.

paragraphs: Self-supervised models turn inputs into representations that capture useful similarity structure without requiring explicit labels during training. Providers can sell access to these representations through inference APIs. The paper studies whether this access lets outsiders extract useful copies of models whose original training was expensive.

The setting differs from extracting a classifier because the API returns high-dimensional representations rather than labels or a small set of prediction scores. The authors construct several attacks and find that directly training on representations obtained from the victim model is query efficient. The resulting models support high accuracy on downstream tasks, showing that extraction can recover practically useful representational behavior.

The paper then evaluates existing model-extraction defenses and finds them inadequate for this setting and difficult to adapt to self-supervised learning. Its central finding is that representation-serving APIs create a distinct protection problem. The same rich outputs that make one pretrained model useful across tasks also provide information that the studied extraction methods can exploit.
icml-2022-on-the-difficulty-of-defending.tldr: Representation outputs enable query-efficient extraction of self-supervised models, while existing defenses prove inadequate in the studied setting.

paragraphs: Directed acyclic graphs describe structures with dependencies but no directed cycles, including candidate neural architectures and probabilistic graphical models. Many learning-based optimization systems encode each graph as a vector before searching for better structures. Popular encoders process nodes in dependency order, waiting until every predecessor has been processed, which prevents simultaneous processing across all nodes.

PACE introduces an attention-based encoder that processes nodes simultaneously and encodes graphs in parallel. The contribution targets a core component of graph optimization: constructing the representations that downstream search procedures use. Faster encoding matters for both training the representation model and applying it while exploring candidate structures.

Experiments evaluate PACE through optimization routines that search using its learned embeddings. It improves effectiveness over earlier sequential encoders while substantially increasing training and inference speed. The learned encoding spaces are also smooth in ways that benefit downstream optimization. These results connect parallel processing with useful representations, showing that the speed improvement accompanies better search behavior in the evaluated applications.
icml-2022-pace-a-parallelizable-computat.tldr: PACE encodes directed acyclic graphs in parallel, improving speed and the usefulness of embeddings for graph-structure optimization.

paragraphs: Visual program induction generates programs that describe observed scenes. The paper argues that fixed, non-parametric primitives limit how much visual detail such programs can express. Parametric functions offer more flexibility, but introduce many possible function variants and complicated dependencies among functions, making program generation harder.

The proposed solution modularizes functions. Each parametric function receives a self-contained neural module with multiple heads to cover its variants. The method also introduces a hierarchical heterogeneous Monte Carlo tree search algorithm, H2MCTS. During training, this search supplies high-quality uncorrelated supervision to address complex function correlations; during testing, it serves as an efficient way to search for programs.

The authors evaluate the method on three visual program induction datasets involving parametric primitives. It substantially outperforms the compared leading baselines in program accuracy. The findings support handling richer visual descriptions through a combination of modular neural representations and structured search, with the same search machinery contributing both training guidance and test-time program discovery.
icml-2022-parametric-visual-program-indu.tldr: Modular neural functions and hierarchical tree search improve generation of parametric programs that describe detailed visual scenes.

paragraphs: Dataset condensation replaces a large training collection with a small synthesized dataset intended to support efficient learning. This paper investigates whether that efficiency mechanism also brings privacy benefits. The motivation is that existing private data generators can be expensive to train or produce data with weak generalization performance.

The authors connect condensation to differential privacy by studying the influence of an individual raw sample. They prove, first for linear feature extractors and then with an extension to nonlinear ones, that this influence on the trained network’s parameter distribution is limited by O(m/n). Here, m synthesized samples are produced from n raw samples, with n much larger than m. The statement concerns individual influence under the analyzed setup.

The empirical study examines visual privacy and membership privacy, including attacks based on losses and likelihoods. These evaluations support privacy benefits for condensed data alongside its intended training efficiency. The contribution combines an influence bound with attack-based evidence; the phrase “privacy for free” refers to privacy benefits arising from a procedure originally designed for another purpose.
icml-2022-privacy-for-free-how-does-data.tldr: Dataset condensation offers privacy benefits supported by bounds on individual-sample influence and evaluations against membership-inference attacks.

paragraphs: When an agent sees only part of its environment, its latest observation may not reveal the underlying state. Remembering history can help, but learning in general partially observable environments faces severe statistical and computational difficulties. This paper identifies a structured subclass in which the latent state can be decoded from only the most recent m steps of history.

That short-history decoding condition is the key assumption. The authors establish upper and lower sample-complexity bounds for learning near-optimal policies, considering both tabular environments and settings with enormous observation spaces. For rich observations, they develop algorithms using a new moment-matching approach to exploit the available short-term state information.

In the rich-observation setting, the resulting sample complexity scales exponentially with memory length m rather than with the problem horizon, and it does not depend on the number of observations. Short memory therefore suffices for reinforcement learning in this subclass. The significance lies in replacing dependence on a potentially long history with dependence on the short window that actually identifies the latent state.
icml-2022-provable-reinforcement-learnin.tldr: When recent history decodes latent states, reinforcement learning can use short memory with guarantees independent of observation-space size.

paragraphs: A counterfactual explanation describes changes that would produce a desired model outcome. Its advice may become invalid when the model is retrained or its hyperparameters change. This paper tackles that reliability problem for tree ensembles, whose non-smooth behavior and potentially substantial changes after retraining make robust explanations difficult to construct.

The authors introduce Counterfactual Stability, a metric intended to estimate how well a counterfactual will survive model changes. They establish desirable theoretical properties for the metric and use it in RobX. Starting from an explanation produced by any base counterfactual method, RobX iteratively refines the candidate to seek greater stability.

Across benchmark datasets, RobX produces substantially more robust counterfactuals than the compared methods, with nearly 100% validity after the actual model changes evaluated. Its explanations also score as more realistic using local outlier factor. The results support stability-guided refinement as a way to improve existing explanation methods, with the near-perfect validity figure describing the tested changes rather than every possible future model.
icml-2022-robust-counterfactual-explanat.tldr: RobX refines counterfactual explanations for tree ensembles to improve their validity after model changes and their measured realism.

paragraphs: Physical predictions should respond consistently when a scene is rotated or translated. SE(3) equivariance encodes that requirement in a model. Building expressive equivariant networks can be computationally expensive, so this paper studies how graph neural networks can represent geometric information efficiently while respecting these transformations.

The framework introduces complete local coordinate frames that themselves transform equivariantly. Each frame is an orthonormal basis, allowing tensor information of a given order to be projected onto it. The construction is designed to avoid losing directional information and to maintain completeness. Because the frames are built using cross-product operations, the authors present them as an efficient foundation for approximating geometric quantities.

The method is evaluated on modeling Newtonian mechanics and generating equilibrium molecular conformations. Across the two types of datasets, it achieves best or competitive performance. These results support local frames as a useful approach to balancing expressiveness and computation in geometric learning, with physical symmetry built directly into how the network represents information.
icml-2022-se-3-equivariant-graph-neural-.tldr: Complete local coordinate frames provide an efficient way to build expressive graph networks that respect three-dimensional rotations and translations.

paragraphs: A controllable system can be moved to any state through suitable control inputs. Many real systems only partly satisfy that description: some state variables evolve independently of the controls. This paper studies a broad class of partially controllable linear systems whose dependencies follow an underlying sparsity pattern.

The authors first establish structural conditions that identify which state variables are irrelevant to optimal control. This distinction matters because being unable to control a variable and having no need to consider it are different questions. The analysis characterizes irrelevance through the system’s structure, providing a basis for concentrating learning on the information that optimal control requires.

The algorithmic contribution adapts soft-thresholding and semiparametric least-squares methods from high-dimensional statistics to exploit that sparsity. The resulting finite-sample guarantees substantially improve on those based on certainty-equivalent control, and simulations corroborate the theoretical improvements. The findings show how structural knowledge about partially controllable systems can translate into stronger guarantees for learning to control them from limited data.
icml-2022-sparsity-in-partially-controll.tldr: Exploiting sparse dependencies in partially controllable linear systems identifies irrelevant state variables and improves finite-sample control guarantees.

paragraphs: Forecasting many related time series requires more than predicting a separate value for each one. Decision-making also needs uncertainty about how their values may vary together. TACTiS targets this joint predictive distribution, aiming to represent dependencies across a high-dimensional collection of time-varying quantities.

The model uses a transformer with an attention-based decoder. The authors prove that the decoder learns to mimic properties of non-parametric copulas, which describe dependence within a joint distribution. This provides a foundation for modeling relationships among predicted quantities. The architecture supports hundreds of time series and accommodates data whose observations are neither aligned across series nor sampled at uniform intervals.

TACTiS handles both forecasting future values and interpolating values within observed time spans, and it adapts to missing data during training. Experiments demonstrate these capabilities and report state-of-the-art predictions on multiple real-world datasets. The contribution combines joint uncertainty modeling with flexibility for irregular observations, allowing a single approach to address several common time-series estimation settings.
icml-2022-tactis-transformer-attentional.tldr: TACTiS models joint uncertainty across many time series while supporting forecasting, interpolation, irregular sampling, and missing data.
